label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
# The Coolroom Died On Cup Day: A Letter To Jonno

Jonno,

You've messaged me four times about the coolroom story. Four. Mate, you live in London now, you've got a Monzo card and you said "brilliant" unironically on the phone last month. You don't get to be this invested in a Melbourne bistro coolroom anymore. But since you won't let it go and I can't be bothered typing it out on my phone, here it is. Everyone else reading this (hi Mum), this is for Jonno, but you can stay.

Set the scene. Tuesday the 3rd of November, Cup Day. We've got 140 booked for lunch. Set menu, three courses, everyone in fascinators and their good shoes, half of them already two proseccos deep before they sit down. It's the biggest lunch of the year and you know it is because you've done it with me. Remember the year you burnt your forearm on the salamander and kept going because you "didn't want to lose momentum"? That energy. Except you weren't there, and Raff was off too, so it was me running the pass. Just me. Captain of the ship.

I rock up at 6.40am. Walk into the coolroom to grab the butter. Something feels off straight away, like when you walk into your house and you can tell someone's been in. I look at the thermometer. 11 degrees.

Eleven, Jonno.

That's not a coolroom, that's a nice spring afternoon. The compressor had carked it at some point overnight and everything in there had been slowly getting comfy for who knows how many hours. I stood there for a solid ten seconds just looking at it like if I stared hard enough it'd drop back to 3.

First call was Wally from Coldline. Lovely bloke, very calm, completely useless to me that day through no fault of his own. The part had to come from Sydney and he couldn't get out till Wednesday. Wednesday. So that's that.

Second call was Phil. You know how Phil is. I explain the whole situation, compressor's dead, 140 covers, no fridge guy till tomorrow, and there's this pause and then he goes "just make it work mate." And hung up. Which, look, I've got to admire the confidence, but that's not a plan. That's a vibe. You can't put a vibe in the fridge.

So we made it work.

Everything that could fit went into the two undercounters and the bar fridge. If you've never tried to Tetris a full coolroom into two undercounters and a bar fridge, don't. It doesn't go. The bar fridge had cream sitting next to the Coronas. Prep containers stacked like a Jenga tower that was one door slam away from disaster. Every time someone opened it you'd hear me yell "GENTLY" from across the kitchen.

That still left a heap of stuff, including the beef shin for the main, so I went next door to Marta's. Marta, absolute legend, said we could have half her walk-in. She didn't even hesitate. But she's a businesswoman, Jonno. Nothing is free. She's charging me in "croissant credit," which I've worked out means I owe her about three weeks of staff meal. Her staff are eating better than ours right now. I made her barista a beef cheek ragu last Thursday and he looked at me like I'd saved his life.

Getting the beef to Marta's is the bit you would've lost your mind at. Me and Benny, 30kg of beef shin, the milk crate trolley (the shit one, you know the one), down the laneway, in the rain. Because of course it was raining. It's Cup Day, it's Melbourne, it's always raining. Halfway down, one of the wheels just comes off. Pings off into the gutter. So now we're half dragging, half carrying this lopsided trolley full of beef, Benny's swearing, I'm swearing, and there's water running down the back of my jacket. Took us way too long. I'm still finding gravel in my clogs.

Meanwhile Kev, our dishy, who is an absolute weapon by the way, gets sent to the servo for ice. He comes back with 14 bags and fills up the old esky out the back (yes, that esky, the one with your name still written on the lid in texta). He reckons the servo guy looked at him buying 14 bags of ice at 8am on Cup Day and asked if we were having a party. Kev said yes. Technically not wrong.

Stock-wise we lost about $1,800. Mostly dairy and the duck legs, which hurt, because those duck legs were beautiful and I'd been looking forward to them all week. Binned the lot. Didn't risk it. Not poisoning 140 people in their race day outfits, that's not the headline I want.

Then service.

And this is the bit I can't really explain, but honestly it was the best service we did all year. I don't know what it was. Everyone was locked in. Nobody whinged. Benny was cooking like he had something to prove. Kev was running ice and plates and clean pans and somehow doing all three at once. The floor staff kept the punters happy and didn't tell them a thing. Nobody out front had a clue we were running a 140-cover lunch off two undercounters, a bar fridge, an esky and someone else's walk-in.

Well. Almost nobody.

Lady on table 9 waves over one of the floor staff and asks, totally straight-faced, if the beef was "free range from the laneway." She'd seen me and Benny out the window, in the rain, wrestling a three-wheeled trolley full of meat past the bins. Our waiter, bless her, said "only the finest." I nearly died.

Then at 12.15 we ran out of space for the panna cotta, and with the temps all over the place I wasn't confident they'd set right anyway, so I 86'd it. Dessert became "affogato with whatever." Whatever being a scoop of gelato we had, a shot, and a crumbled biscuit or a bit of praline depending on what was left. People LOVED it. Way more than they ever loved the panna cotta. Multiple tables asked if it was a new menu item. I've been making that panna cotta for two years, Jonno. Two years. And the thing that gets compliments is a bit of ice cream with coffee poured on it that I threw together in a panic. The universe has a sense of humour.

Speaking of which. My horse in the staff sweep was called Ice Cold Lad. I'm not making that up. Ice Cold Lad. On the day the coolroom died. And it came second last. Didn't even have the decency to come last so I could at least get a laugh out of it. Second last. Just mediocre. The universe is taking the piss and it wants me to know about it.

Wally came Wednesday, swapped the part, and the coolroom's been sitting at a crisp 2 degrees ever since like nothing happened. Smug thing. I check it every morning now. I've got trust issues.

If there's one thing I learned, it's that bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. That's it. That's the whole industry. You can have all the fancy gear you want, but at some point it's going to be you and a mate dragging beef down a laneway in the rain and making it work because the alternative is telling 140 people in fascinators to go home.

Which brings me to you. Because I've been thinking about it, and you would've cried. Old you wouldn't have. Old Jonno would've been out there with us, probably carrying the beef on his shoulder like a lunatic. But London Jonno? London Jonno who complains when the tube's a bit warm and has started saying "cheers" when he means thank you? London Jonno would've seen 11 degrees on that thermometer and needed a sit down and a cup of tea. London's made you soft, mate. It's broken you. I say this with love.

Anyway, that's the story. Coolroom's fixed, nobody got sick, I owe Marta a lot of lunches, and the affogato might be staying on the menu.

Your name's still on the esky. Your spot on grill's still there too, though Benny's getting real comfortable on it, so don't leave it too long.

Come home ya flog.

— your mate on the pass
